name: Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix
description: Master the Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix position in BJJ. High-percentage blood choke finish with bilateral arm control, setup mechanics, and defense.
summary: The Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix is a high-percentage blood choke finished from crucifix control, where both of the opponent's arms are isolated—one by a leg triangle, the other by hand—leaving the neck undefended for a carotid strangle.
overview:
The Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix exploits the defining advantage of the crucifix position: complete bilateral arm isolation. With both of the opponent's arms trapped—one by a leg triangle configuration and the other by hand or overhook control—the neck becomes almost entirely undefended, creating a finishing scenario with one of the highest success rates of any choke setup in competitive grappling.

The primary technical challenge lies in transitioning from arm control to choking grip without compromising positional integrity. The attacker must release control of the far arm to thread the choking arm under the opponent's chin, creating a brief vulnerability window where the defender may free a hand for neck defense. Timing this transition—and having secondary controls ready—separates successful finishes from scrambles back to neutral crucifix.

Unlike the standard RNC from back control, the crucifix variant benefits from the opponent's severely limited hip mobility and inability to create defensive angles. The trapped arms cannot generate the frames needed for escape, and the opponent's awareness of their vulnerability often produces reactions that further expose the neck. Advanced practitioners use the choke threat to set up arm attacks, creating a submission chain where defending one threat opens another.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate to 30 seconds with proper release

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper forearm placement
Carotid artery injury from excessive force

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training. Never snap or jerk the choke. Partner should have full awareness of pressure building.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (say 'tap' or make any verbal sound)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body or mat
Going limp or loss of consciousness
Any distress signal or unusual sound
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm upon tap signal
Remove hooks and leg triangle trapping the arm
Gently guide partner to side-lying recovery position
Monitor consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds
If partner was unconscious, keep them lying down until fully alert
Never allow unconscious partner to stand immediately
training_restrictions: Never use competition speed or intensity in drilling
Never apply the choke to the trachea or windpipe
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with at least one hand
Stop immediately if partner makes any distress sound
Never hold a choke past the tap for any reason
Beginners must practice with extremely slow progression only

variations_and_setups.description: Instead of the classic figure-four behind the head, clasp both hands together palm-to-palm with the choking forearm under the chin. This grip is faster to secure when the defender gets a hand to their neck, as you can lock the grip around the defensive hand and still generate sufficient carotid compression.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the defender manages to get their freed hand to their neck before you can lock the figure-four, trapping the defensive hand inside the choke

variations_and_setups.description: Apply the choking forearm across the opponent's jaw rather than under the chin. With both arms trapped in crucifix, the jaw pressure creates extreme discomfort that either forces a tap directly or causes the opponent to lift their chin to relieve pressure, opening space for the forearm to slide underneath into a clean blood choke.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When the opponent aggressively tucks their chin and you cannot thread the forearm underneath cleanly

variations_and_setups.description: Rather than threading the full forearm under the chin, use just the wrist and lower forearm in a compressed choking position. Grip the back of your own head with the choking hand and use the non-choking arm to push the opponent's head forward into the choke. This variation requires less space to lock and works well when the opponent keeps their chin tight.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When there is limited space under the chin and you cannot achieve the full depth needed for a standard RNC grip

attacker.name: Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix Attacker
attacker.description: Complete guide to finishing the Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix. Step-by-step execution, grip transitions, and counter-responses for this dominant blood choke.
attacker.overview: Executing the Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix capitalizes on the most advantageous choking position in grappling—both opponent arms trapped with full neck exposure. The critical skill is managing the transition from dual arm control to choking grip while maintaining enough positional integrity to prevent escape. The crucifix eliminates the standard two-on-one hand defense that makes back control RNC so difficult, transforming a typically contested submission into a high-percentage finish when the transition is properly timed and executed.
key_principles: Maintain leg triangle pressure on the trapped arm throughout the entire choke sequence—this is your positional anchor that makes the finish possible
Minimize the transition window when releasing the far arm to thread the choking arm—pre-position the choking arm close to the neck before releasing
Thread the choking arm palm-down along the jawline, using the chin as a guide rather than forcing under it
Secure the figure-four lock behind the head, not behind the neck, and press the head forward to prevent chin tuck defense
Apply squeeze through shoulder retraction and chest expansion rather than bicep flexion for deeper, more efficient carotid compression
Keep your head tight against the opponent's temple to prevent them from turning into the choke and creating defensive space
setup_requirements: Established crucifix control with opponent's near arm fully trapped in leg triangle configuration with constant inward pressure
Far arm controlled by wrist grip or overhook preventing immediate neck defense upon release
Opponent positioned on their side or back with limited hip mobility and compromised base
Clear path to the neck confirmed—opponent's chin is accessible or can be pried open through angle adjustment
Body weight settled through hips onto opponent's torso preventing explosive escape during transition

execution_steps.description: Verify that the leg triangle is locked tight on the near arm with constant inward pressure. Test by feeling for any slack in the trap—if the opponent can rotate their trapped arm even slightly, tighten the triangle before proceeding. Settle your weight through your hips onto the opponent's upper back and shoulder to anchor the position.

execution_steps.action: Secure Far Arm and Assess Neck Access
execution_steps.description: Control the opponent's far arm with a strong wrist grip or deep overhook. Use this moment to assess the neck—check chin position, neck angle, and available space to thread your forearm. If the chin is deeply tucked with no entry angle, consider switching to an arm attack first to force the chin up before reattempting.

execution_steps.action: Release Far Arm and Thread Choking Arm
execution_steps.description: This is the critical transition moment. Release control of the far arm and immediately drive your choking-side forearm toward the opponent's neck, threading it palm-down along their jawline. Speed matters here—the defender has a brief 1-2 second window to bring their freed hand to their neck for defense before you can lock the grip.

Guide your forearm under the chin by using the blade of your wrist against the jawline as a wedge. Keep your elbow tight against the opponent's chest to eliminate space. The crook of your elbow should align with the center of the throat so the radius compresses one carotid and the bicep compresses the other.

execution_steps.action: Lock the Figure-Four Behind the Head
execution_steps.description: Bring your non-choking hand to grip your own bicep on the choking arm, forming the classic figure-four configuration. Place the non-choking hand behind the opponent's skull, not behind the neck. Press the head forward with your palm to drive the neck into the choking forearm and eliminate any remaining chin tuck defense.

Squeeze by retracting your shoulders and expanding your chest rather than flexing your bicep. Keep your head tight against the opponent's temple to prevent turning escape. In training, apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds. A properly positioned RNC from crucifix produces unconsciousness within 4-6 seconds at full compression, so controlled application is essential.

common_counters.counter: Freed hand immediately goes to neck defense upon far arm release
common_counters.your_response: Anticipate this by threading the choking arm as rapidly as possible during the transition window. If the hand reaches the neck, use your non-choking hand to strip the grip by peeling fingers from your wrist starting from the pinky side before they establish a two-on-one defense.

common_counters.counter: Explosive bridge and turn toward attacker during transition
common_counters.your_response: Maintain heavy hip pressure and keep your head against theirs to prevent rotation. If they begin to turn, accelerate the choke entry rather than resettling—the turning motion often further exposes the neck as their chin lifts.

common_counters.counter: Opponent extracts trapped arm from leg triangle during choke transition
common_counters.your_response: If the arm is partially out, immediately convert to standard back control hooks and continue the RNC from conventional back position. Do not attempt to re-establish crucifix once the choke sequence has begun—transition is more efficient than recovery.

common_counters.counter: Aggressive chin tuck and shoulder raise to block forearm entry
common_counters.your_response: Use the non-choking hand to pry the chin up from the opposite side. Alternatively, apply the choke over the chin—with both arms trapped, jaw pressure alone can force a tap or create space under the chin as the opponent lifts to relieve pressure.

common_errors.error: Releasing far arm control before the choking arm is pre-positioned near the neck
common_errors.consequence: Gives the opponent a free hand for neck defense well before the choke is in position, converting a dominant position into a contested scramble
common_errors.correction: Pre-position the choking arm close to the neck before releasing the far arm. The release and thread should be nearly simultaneous with minimal gap between them.

common_errors.error: Placing the forearm across the trachea instead of the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Creates a windpipe crush that is painful but does not produce a blood choke, giving the opponent more time to escape and risking serious tracheal injury
common_errors.correction: Align the crook of the elbow with the center of the throat so the radius and ulna compress the carotid arteries on each side. Adjust angle by sliding the arm deeper if the pressure is on the front of the throat.

common_errors.error: Loosening the leg triangle while focusing attention on the choke
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts their trapped arm and regains defensive capability, turning a dominant finishing position into a back control scramble
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant inward squeeze with legs throughout the entire choke sequence. The leg triangle is your positional foundation—never sacrifice it for the choke.

common_errors.error: Locking the figure-four behind the neck instead of behind the head
common_errors.consequence: Reduces mechanical advantage, allows effective chin tuck defense, and creates a neck crank rather than a clean blood choke
common_errors.correction: Place the non-choking hand behind the skull and press the head forward. This drives the neck into the choking forearm and eliminates the chin tuck escape.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with bicep flexion instead of shoulder retraction
common_errors.consequence: Rapid forearm fatigue without sufficient arterial compression—the choke feels tight but does not produce unconsciousness efficiently
common_errors.correction: Drive the squeeze by pulling your elbows together and expanding your chest. Think of squeezing shoulder blades together rather than curling your arm.

common_errors.error: Rushing choke application in training without progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Risk of injury through sudden blood flow interruption or tracheal damage from imprecise forearm placement under speed
common_errors.correction: Apply the choke slowly and progressively in training, giving your partner time to tap. Competition speed should never be used in drilling or positional sparring.

training_progressions.focus: Crucifix control and arm transition mechanics
training_progressions.description: Practice establishing crucifix and transitioning from dual arm control to single arm release with a cooperative partner. Focus on minimizing the window between releasing the far arm and threading the choking arm. No finishing—repetitions of the entry transition only until the movement becomes fluid and automatic.

training_progressions.focus: Forearm placement and figure-four lock precision
training_progressions.description: From pre-set crucifix position, practice threading the choking arm and locking the figure-four with correct placement behind the head. Partner provides feedback on pressure location and whether compression is on the carotid arteries or trachea. Apply only light squeeze to verify correct targeting without risk.

Partner defends with specific counters at increasing intensity: chin tuck defense at 50%, freed hand to neck at 75%, explosive bridging at 90%. Attacker practices timing the transition and adjusting to each defensive response while maintaining crucifix leg triangle integrity throughout.

Start from established crucifix position with full resistance from both players. Attacker works to finish the RNC while defender works to escape or prevent the choke. Three-minute rounds with position resets. Track finish rate across sessions to measure progress and identify persistent gaps.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix primarily attack?
flashcards.answer: The RNC targets the carotid arteries on both sides of the neck, compressing them between the forearm and bicep to restrict blood flow to the brain. The crook of the elbow aligns with the center of the throat so the radius bone compresses one carotid artery and the bicep compresses the other. This produces cerebral ischemia and unconsciousness within 4-8 seconds of a properly locked choke, making correct arterial targeting essential for both effectiveness and safety.

flashcards.question: What is the critical transition window and how do you minimize defensive opportunities during it?
flashcards.answer: The transition window is the moment when you release control of the far arm to thread the choking arm under the chin. During this 1-2 second window, the opponent's freed hand can reach their neck for defense. Minimize this by pre-positioning the choking arm close to the neck before releasing, making the release and thread nearly simultaneous. Speed and preparation during this window determine whether the choke succeeds or becomes a contested grip fight.

flashcards.question: Your opponent aggressively tucks their chin as you thread the choking arm—what adjustments do you make?
flashcards.answer: First, use the non-choking hand to push the chin up from the opposite side or pry under it with your wrist blade along the jawline as a wedge. If the chin remains locked, apply the choke over the chin—from crucifix with both arms trapped, the jaw pressure creates extreme discomfort that often forces the opponent to lift their chin voluntarily, creating space for the forearm to slide underneath into a clean blood choke position.

flashcards.question: What is the correct forearm placement to ensure a blood choke rather than an air choke?
flashcards.answer: The crook of the elbow must align with the center of the opponent's throat so that the radius and ulna compress one carotid artery while the bicep compresses the other. If the forearm sits across the front of the trachea, it creates an air choke that is less effective and significantly more dangerous to the training partner. Confirm correct placement by checking that pressure is felt on the sides of the neck, not the front. Adjust by sliding the arm deeper if needed.

flashcards.question: How should you release the Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix immediately upon receiving a tap signal?
flashcards.answer: Immediately open the figure-four lock and remove the choking arm from the neck. Release the leg triangle to free the trapped arm. Allow the opponent to return to a neutral position. Monitor their consciousness and breathing for at least 30 seconds after release. If they lost consciousness, keep them in a side-lying recovery position and do not allow them to stand until they are fully alert and responsive. Never hold the choke past the tap for any reason.

flashcards.question: What are the indicators that the choke is properly positioned and will produce a finish?
flashcards.answer: Key indicators include the opponent's face rapidly changing color, involuntary body tension followed by progressive relaxation, the opponent's movements becoming slower and less coordinated, and the feeling of arterial pulse against your forearm diminishing. In training, a properly locked choke typically produces a tap within 2-3 seconds. If you are squeezing hard but the opponent shows no distress after 5 seconds, your forearm placement is likely off-center and needs adjustment.

flashcards.question: Why is maintaining leg triangle pressure during the choke attempt essential to the finish?
flashcards.answer: The leg triangle trapping the near arm is the positional foundation that makes the crucifix RNC viable. If the leg triangle loosens, the opponent extracts their trapped arm and immediately gains defensive capability—they can create frames, fight the choking arm with two hands, and generate escape momentum. Maintaining constant leg pressure ensures the opponent remains defenseless throughout the choke sequence, preserving the asymmetric advantage that defines this position and its high finish rate.

flashcards.question: Your opponent gets their freed hand inside your choking grip before the figure-four is locked—how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: Use your non-choking hand to isolate and strip their defensive hand by peeling fingers from your wrist or forearm, working from the pinky side. If the grip is too established to strip, switch to an arm attack on the now-exposed defending arm—reaching to defend the neck pulls their arm away from their body into vulnerable positions for kimura or armbar. This creates a submission chain where defending the choke opens a different attack.

flashcards.question: What distinguishes the RNC finish from crucifix versus standard back control in terms of defensive options available to the opponent?
flashcards.answer: From standard back control, the opponent has both arms free for defense, enabling two-on-one grip fighting, active hand fighting on the choking arm, and frame creation against the head. From crucifix, at minimum one arm is completely trapped by the leg triangle and the other is controlled or briefly freed during transition. This eliminates the two-on-one defense entirely and reduces defensive options to single-hand fighting and chin tuck, dramatically increasing the finish rate compared to conventional back control RNC attempts.

flashcards.question: What training speed should you use when drilling this submission and why is it particularly important from crucifix?
flashcards.answer: Always drill with slow, progressive application—3-5 seconds minimum to build pressure in training. The RNC from crucifix is particularly dangerous because the opponent has severely limited defensive capacity and the choke can lock fully before they have time to tap. Never use competition speed during drilling. The combination of positional dominance and rapid blood flow restriction means unconsciousness can occur within seconds of a properly locked choke, making controlled and progressive application absolutely essential for partner safety.

defender.name: Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix Defender
defender.description: Defend the Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix. Recognition cues, defensive timing windows, hand fighting techniques, and escape strategies from this dominant control.
defender.overview: Defending the Rear Naked Choke from Crucifix demands immediate action within an extremely limited defensive window. With one arm trapped in the attacker's leg triangle and the other being released for the choke transition, your defensive options are severely constrained compared to standard RNC defense. The primary survival strategy centers on exploiting the brief moment when the attacker releases your far arm to thread the choking grip—this transition window is your single best opportunity to establish neck defense or begin escaping the crucifix entirely. Recognition of the choke setup before it locks is the most important defensive skill, as a fully secured RNC from crucifix with both arms compromised is nearly impossible to escape.
key_principles: Recognize the choke transition immediately—when the attacker releases your far arm, they are committing to the RNC and you must react within 1-2 seconds
Rush your freed hand to your neck the instant it is released, creating a barrier before the choking arm threads under your chin
Tuck your chin hard against your chest and raise your shoulder on the threatened side to create a physical barrier against forearm entry
Work to free the trapped arm from the leg triangle using hip movement and angle changes—a freed arm transforms your defensive options entirely
Maintain calm breathing and controlled defensive movements rather than explosive panic reactions that waste energy and tighten the position
If the choke locks fully with the figure-four secured, tap immediately rather than fighting a submission that has virtually zero escape rate from this position
recognition_cues: Attacker shifts their hand positioning on your far arm, loosening the wrist grip or overhook in preparation for releasing it to thread the choke
Attacker adjusts their body angle to align their choking arm with your neck, often bringing their chest and head closer to your temple
Weight distribution changes as the attacker prepares to commit their arm to the choke, often becoming heavier on one side of your upper body
You feel the far arm control loosen or disappear entirely, immediately signaling that the choke transition has begun and your defensive window is open

defensive_options.action: Freed hand to neck defense—grip your own collar or place hand at throat level to block forearm entry
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when attacker releases far arm control—this is your highest priority action within the first 1-2 seconds
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the choke from locking, forcing attacker to strip your grip or re-establish arm control, buying time for further escape
defensive_options.risk: If you focus only on hand defense without working to escape the crucifix, the attacker will eventually strip your grip and reattempt

defensive_options.action: Explosive bridge and turn during transition window to disrupt crucifix structure
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker releases your far arm and commits to threading the choke—they have voluntarily reduced positional control for the attack
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the crucifix position entirely, may allow you to turn to guard, recover half guard, or reach a scramble position
defensive_options.risk: If the bridge fails, you may have wasted critical energy and the attacker will tighten control before you can reset defensively

defensive_options.action: Extract trapped arm from leg triangle while attacker's attention is split between leg control and choke application
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits to the choking grip and their focus shifts from maintaining the leg triangle to finishing the neck attack
defensive_options.if_successful: Frees both arms for defense, converting the position to standard back control which has significantly more established escape options
defensive_options.risk: Focusing on arm extraction while ignoring an actively tightening choke can result in being submitted before the arm clears the triangle

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck with shoulder raise to physically block the forearm from sliding under the jaw
defensive_options.when_to_use: As you feel the forearm approaching your neck—this is a stalling defense to buy time for other escape actions
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the choking arm from threading cleanly under the chin, forcing the attacker to use a hand to pry the chin or reposition
defensive_options.risk: Chin tuck alone does not escape the position and the attacker can apply the choke over the chin for a jaw crush that forces the chin up

escape_paths: Bridge and turn during choke transition window to disrupt crucifix and recover guard position
Extract trapped arm through incremental hip movement and convert to standard back control escape sequence
Two-on-one grip fight the choking arm while simultaneously working to free legs from crucifix configuration

favorable_outcomes.how: Exploit the transition window when attacker releases far arm to bridge explosively and turn into them, disrupting the crucifix structure and working to close guard before the attacker re-establishes dominant control or completes the choke

common_errors.error: Failing to immediately use the freed hand for neck defense when the far arm is released
common_errors.consequence: The choking arm threads under the chin unopposed and the figure-four locks before any defensive action can be initiated
common_errors.correction: The instant you feel your far arm released, your hand goes directly to your neck or collar—this reaction must be drilled until completely automatic with zero hesitation

common_errors.error: Relying solely on chin tuck while ignoring positional escape from the crucifix
common_errors.consequence: The attacker pries the chin up or applies the choke over the jaw, and you remain trapped in crucifix with steadily decreasing defensive options
common_errors.correction: Use chin tuck as a temporary stalling measure while simultaneously working to extract the trapped arm through hip movement or bridge out of the crucifix position entirely

common_errors.error: Panicking and making large explosive movements that telegraph escape intentions
common_errors.consequence: The attacker anticipates your escape direction and adjusts accordingly, often tightening leg triangle control and accelerating the choke entry
common_errors.correction: Combine multiple small coordinated defensive actions: chin tuck plus freed hand to neck plus incremental hip movement for arm extraction, working systematically rather than explosively

common_errors.error: Continuing to fight a fully locked RNC with figure-four secured instead of tapping
common_errors.consequence: Loss of consciousness within 4-8 seconds of a properly positioned blood choke, creating unnecessary medical risk in training
common_errors.correction: If the figure-four is locked behind your head and the squeeze begins, tap immediately. The RNC from crucifix with both arms compromised has virtually zero escape rate once fully secured—preserving your health for the next round is the correct decision.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the attacker is transitioning from crucifix control to the Rear Naked Choke attempt?
flashcards.answer: Key recognition cues include the attacker loosening or shifting their grip on your far arm, their body angle changing to align the choking arm with your neck, and a weight shift as they prepare to commit. The most definitive signal is feeling your far arm released entirely—at this point the choke transition is actively happening and you have 1-2 seconds to establish neck defense before the forearm reaches your chin. Early recognition dramatically improves defensive success rates.

flashcards.question: What is the safest response if the choke is fully locked with the figure-four secured behind your head?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately using any available signal—verbal tap, hand tap on the attacker's body or the mat, or foot tap on the mat. A properly locked RNC from crucifix produces unconsciousness within 4-8 seconds and has virtually zero escape rate when both arms are compromised by the crucifix configuration. Fighting a locked choke from this position wastes energy and risks loss of consciousness. Tapping to a fully secured submission from the most dominant finishing position in grappling is the correct and safe decision.

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available when the attacker threads their forearm under your chin but has not locked the figure-four?
flashcards.answer: If the forearm is under the chin but the figure-four is not locked, use your freed hand for two-on-one defense—grip the choking wrist and pull it away from your neck while turning your chin toward the crook of the elbow to reduce compression. Simultaneously work to extract the trapped arm from the leg triangle through hip movement. If you can strip the choking grip, immediately address the crucifix position before the attacker reattempts. Time is critical because once the figure-four locks, effective defense becomes nearly impossible.

flashcards.question: Why is the transition moment when the attacker releases your far arm the most important defensive window?
flashcards.answer: This is the only moment when the attacker has voluntarily reduced their control over the position—they have released one control point to commit to the choke. This brief window is your best opportunity because you have a free hand for immediate neck defense, the attacker's weight is shifting during the transition creating potential instability, and their attention is split between maintaining the leg triangle trap and threading the choking arm. Every second of delay in exploiting this window decreases your probability of successful defense.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying choke transition cues and building automatic reaction
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes crucifix and slowly initiates the RNC transition at 25% speed. Defender practices recognizing the release of the far arm and immediately bringing the freed hand to neck defense. No resistance from attacker—focus purely on building the automatic recognition-to-defense reaction until there is zero hesitation between feeling the arm released and protecting the neck.

training_progressions.focus: Hand fighting, chin defense, and grip stripping technique
training_progressions.description: From pre-set crucifix with partner applying the choke at 50% speed, practice the full defensive sequence: freed hand to neck, chin tuck, grip stripping from the pinky side, and simultaneous arm extraction attempts. Partner provides verbal feedback on timing and defensive hand positioning. Build proficiency with each individual defensive tool before combining them.

training_progressions.focus: Combining neck defense with positional escape under pressure
training_progressions.description: Partner applies the RNC from crucifix at 75% intensity with increasing speed. Defender combines neck defense with full escape attempts: bridging during transition, arm extraction through hip movement, and guard recovery. Practice transitioning from defense to escape rather than treating them as separate phases. Track which escape paths are most successful against different attacker responses.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance survival and escape under competition conditions
training_progressions.description: Three-minute rounds from crucifix bottom with partner actively attacking the RNC at full intensity. Full resistance from both players. Track survival time and escape rate across sessions. Debrief after each round to identify specific defensive gaps, timing errors, and which recognition cues were missed or acted on too slowly.
